title: Britain’s dependence on London
author: John Burn-Murdoch
question: How much does a national GDP comparison conceal regional concentration?
claim: The UK depends unusually heavily on London in the comparisons shown; removing it lowers GDP per head by a reported 14%.
comparison_denominator: GDP / resident population; remove both regional output and population. This is an accounting exclusion, not a causal secession forecast.
data_coverage_units: Main/expanded plots: OECD regional accounts; PPP-adjusted thousand USD per head; logarithmic scale; UK/Germany/Netherlands/US plus France/Spain/Italy. Growth chart: 2019=100, 2020-2022; ONS/Scottish government.
analysis: Compare within-country distributions and recompute population-weighted national means excluding richest region; then contrast recovery trajectories.
argument_sequence_counterevidence: Aggregate challenge -> regional distribution -> exclusion comparison -> expanded countries -> growth context -> GDP-versus-living-standards caveat. Different boundary choices and country sizes can alter concentration.
chart_role: Three actual assets inspected: regional dotplots plus before/after mean rules; expanded-country plot; London highlighted against grey recovery lines. Bubble-size meaning is not documented by a visible legend.
prose_structure: Claim first; compact comparisons; methodological caveat and acknowledgments follow.
adaptation_feasibility_effort: Medium effort: a bounded one-country regional concentration story can use public GDP/population tables. Cross-country reconstruction is high effort until vintage, territorial grid, PPP base and aggregation are fixed.
licensing: FT prose/graphics remain copyrighted; OECD data terms and individual national-source terms need checking for an actual data release.
unresolved_issues: Exact OECD download/vintage/region mapping and FT transformations absent; 14% not independently reproduced; growth series not downloaded. OECD source family verified, original input not recovered.
craft_lesson: Make the aggregate answer compete with a subgroup view; keep the metric caveat close to the provocative claim. Equal boundaries and explicit weights are prerequisites.

title: Evidence on rent control
author: John Burn-Murdoch
format_length: Four public Bluesky posts; short research synthesis
question: Who gains and who loses under rent control?
claim: Covered tenants can gain while wider housing outcomes can worsen; the thread allows a conditional role for controls alongside supply.
comparison_denominator: Each circle is one study result within an outcome, not one equally independent study across the chart; 112 is the reported review-wide study count, not the denominator of every row.
data_coverage_units: Kholodilin 2024, Journal of Housing Economics 63, 101983, DOI 10.1016/j.jhe.2024.101983. Seven displayed outcome rows; harmful/unclear/beneficial result categories; no effect-size units.
analysis: Direction-of-result evidence display; does not show precision, study quality, sample-size weighting, policy generation or effect magnitude.
argument_sequence_counterevidence: Question -> benefits and adverse spillovers -> conditional caveat -> housing-shortage mechanism -> source. Homelessness row is visibly mixed; policy/context heterogeneity limits universal conclusions.
chart_role: Actual public root-post image inspected. Separated outcome rows keep the covered-tenant benefit visible; jittered colored dots show mixed evidence but overlapping dots prevent exact visual counting.
prose_structure: Question, compact trade-off list, qualification, mechanism, research link.
adaptation_feasibility_effort: Medium/high effort: a research-synthesis story needs outcome-level coding and denominators from the final review; cannot replace that work with an ordinary rent time series or treat sign counts as effect sizes.
licensing: FT chart/prose copyright separate from research rights. Publisher search metadata reports open access/Creative Commons; direct final article fetch failed. Raw data reported available on request, not a verified downloadable open dataset.
unresolved_issues: Final review tables/supplement and dot-to-study coding not recovered. ScienceDirect direct fetch 403. No independent recoding or effect-size synthesis; no claim that all outcomes are adverse.
craft_lesson: Expose both beneficiary and spillover before the conclusion; explicitly name the evidence unit and outcome-specific denominator. A legible synthesis can still overstate generality.

title: Families spend £489 each week - on what?
author: Mona Chalabi
question: How should a household spending average be unpacked?
claim: The headline average needs subgroup and price-basis context.
comparison_denominator: ONS mirror A5: spending shares use total household expenditure; groups rank gross income, not wealth. Regional chart uses pounds per person. Six selected chart categories are renormalized to 100%, not shares of all spending.
data_coverage_units: ONS Family Spending 2013 edition, calendar 2012. Linked A5 mirror: UK, sample 5600 households, weighted 26.41m; pounds/week income boundaries and spending percentages. Housing excludes mortgage interest, council tax and NI rates.
analysis: Inspect subgroup shares and unit changes; first chart has 13 category amounts summing to 488.9 pounds (rounding). A5 thresholds 170 and 1397 are income boundaries, not verified spending levels.
argument_sequence_counterevidence: Average -> time basis -> subgroup comparisons -> definition -> detail. Linked A5 does not support the spending-level comparison using its income thresholds; other original tables were not recovered.
chart_role: All three linked Datawrapper charts rendered/inspected. Main horizontal bars show amount ranking; income chart normalizes six categories; regional bars mix nation/region aggregates and use per-person units.
prose_structure: Numeric introduction; topical subheads; definitions; small observations; commentary.
adaptation_feasibility_effort: Low/medium effort with an already structured current expenditure table; high effort for full 2012 reconstruction. Preserve total-spend denominator and distinguish income, spending and household size.
licensing: ONS-attributed data mirror carries Crown copyright; exact original-table licence not retrieved. Article and Datawrapper rendering rights remain separate; no article/chart copying licensed by this assessment.
unresolved_issues: Data verified for linked A5 and chart payloads only; original ONS 2013 release/list links 404, full tables and historical interactive unresolved. No blanket endorsement of article arithmetic or interpretations.
source_links: S1 S2 S3 S4 S5 S6
craft_lesson: Use everyday categories to make an average matter, then audit every denominator. A 100%-stacked subset can contradict the whole-budget reading even with correct input percentages.

title: UK median weekly pay is £517 - but who earns that?
author: Mona Chalabi
question: Whom does a national pay median describe?
claim: A national median needs subgroup and measurement context.
comparison_denominator: ONS: gross weekly earnings for full-time employee jobs on adult rates, pay unaffected by absence; not take-home income/all workers. Hourly gender gap excludes overtime and uses male pay as denominator.
data_coverage_units: ONS ASHE April 2013 provisional/2012 revised; 1% PAYE employee-job sample. Weekly/hourly GBP; occupation and workplace geography; linked Table13 mirror contains occupation medians.
analysis: Distinguish weekly/hourly and full/part-time estimates; ONS weekly median 517.5; hourly men 13.60/women 12.24 gives 10% below male pay, about 11.1% above female pay in reverse.
argument_sequence_counterevidence: Headline -> definition -> inflation -> subgroup and geographic checks. Official April CPI is 2.4%; the article gives 2.3%. Group medians alone do not identify unequal pay for identical work.
chart_role: Historical ONS cartogram linked through Guardian wrapper; iframe host/visual unavailable in this pass. Described intent is workplace-level exploration; this is not visual verification.
prose_structure: Number-led subheads; brief explanations; data invitation.
adaptation_feasibility_effort: Low/medium effort for a short piece using existing structured earnings tables. Start with one denominator and unit, then one revealing subgroup; high effort if recreating obsolete cartogram.
licensing: ONS data rights separate from Guardian prose/map rights; ONS bulletin footer links OGL v3. Mirror publication does not establish permission for all publisher formatting.
unresolved_issues: Map cannot be assessed visually; linked sheet misleadingly titled National minimum wage but visible Table13 is occupation earnings. Do not copy article gap wording or inflation comparison unchecked.
craft_lesson: Explain the statistic before comparing groups; preserve pay basis, workplace/residence geography and percentage denominator. Concise prose still needs a primary-source audit.

title: Ideological divide between young men and women
author: John Burn-Murdoch
format_length: 31-post thread; short-journalism category, longer than the core four
question: Does a generation-wide political label hide sex differences?
claim: The selected countries show a young male/female divide; explanations are proposed rather than identified causally.
comparison_denominator: Main chart: age 18-29, percent liberal minus percent conservative by sex; US self-identification differs from party-support measures elsewhere; values adjusted for overall-population time trend.
data_coverage_units: Chart credits Gallup/Daniel Cox, Korean/German/US social surveys and British Election Study. Main time spans vary roughly 1980-2023; secondary US chart uses CES 2020. Five chart assets inspected.
analysis: Disaggregate age and sex, compare trajectories and issue items. Different measures, populations and smoothing choices prevent treating these panels as a harmonized causal series.
argument_sequence_counterevidence: Generation puzzle -> disaggregation -> country/issue cases -> proposed mechanisms -> implications -> replies/correction. Thread corrects Korean chart agree/disagree label; original asset still needs that correction alongside it.
chart_role: Small multiples with consistent sex colors and filled separation; issue-level age panels test breadth. Five central assets visually inspected; no claim that all thread media were checked.
prose_structure: Claim-led serial explanation; cases accumulate before mechanism and reader replies.
adaptation_feasibility_effort: Medium effort for one clearly documented survey/item; high for international synthesis. Public GSS/BES portals provide routes, but weights, age bands, questionnaire changes and chart transformations require work.
licensing: FT charts/prose copyrighted. GSS/BES/other surveys have separate access and reuse terms; public portals are not blanket licences for every survey or derived graphic.
unresolved_issues: Underlying exact waves/items, weights, smoothing and all country datasets not downloaded. Main chart combines different constructs; causal speculation and demographic consequences not independently established.
source_links: G1 G2 G3 G4 G5 G6 G7 G8
craft_lesson: Use disaggregation to resolve an apparent contradiction, then separate observed pattern from mechanism. Corrections and cross-country comparability belong beside the chart.

title: Egg prices have quadrupled, chicken has doubled
author: Mona Chalabi / Guardian Design
format_length: Very short journalism plus illustrated graphic
question: How can item prices make inflation tangible?
claim: Selected staple prices increased unevenly over two decades.
comparison_denominator: Paired dollar price for the same item/unit; 2005 versus 2025 labels. Price level ratio and percent change differ; selected goods do not represent a household-weighted CPI basket.
data_coverage_units: Linked BLS average-price page; US retail selected food/energy prices, per pound unless specified (eggs/dozen, electricity/kWh, gasoline and milk/gallon). Ten illustrated pairs visually inspected.
analysis: Endpoint comparison; primary BLS current table is accessible, but exact article endpoint months/vintage and all ten historical pairs not retrieved.
argument_sequence_counterevidence: Familiar purchase -> paired comparison -> purchasing-power implication. Endpoint selection and excluded goods can change impression; no full household-burden estimate follows from selected prices.
chart_role: Actual illustration inspected: two columns, item drawings, dollar labels and explicit unit exceptions. Object sizes dramatize changes; exact reading should use numbers because area/length scaling is not explained.
prose_structure: Short introduction; linked source; graphic carries most comparisons.
adaptation_feasibility_effort: Low/medium using an already structured item-price time series; independently fix endpoint months and units. Reusing illustration style/assets is not necessary to reuse the analytical comparison.
licensing: BLS data are public domain except pre-existing copyrighted images/illustrations; cite BLS. Guardian/Mona Chalabi illustration and article remain separately copyrighted.
unresolved_issues: BLS page is live/current, not a pinned historical extract; endpoint provenance and illustration scaling not independently reproduced. A price story is not a spending-share or real-wage result.
craft_lesson: Make abstract change concrete with stable units; use labeled numbers to anchor illustration. Explain basket and endpoint limits before drawing household-wide conclusions.

title: Regression Analysis
author: Seeing Theory team / Brown University
format_length: Archived interactive teaching chapter; not journalism
question: How do observations determine a regression fit?
claim: Learning objective: understand OLS and inspect data configurations rather than trust summary statistics alone.
comparison_denominator: Four Anscombe datasets, 11 observations each; synthetic/demonstration coordinates, not a representative population. Also Iris traits and ANOVA examples.
data_coverage_units: Hosted anscombe.csv retrieved: X1-X4/Y1-Y4, 11 rows; iris.csv retrieved, trait columns and species labels. No new observational-data collection needed.
analysis: OLS minimizes squared residuals; quartet selection exposes contrasting point patterns with similar fitted summaries.
argument_sequence_counterevidence: Definition -> choose data -> visual response -> parameters/formulas; then correlation and ANOVA. Identical summaries do not imply a suitable linear model; this does not teach causal identification by itself.
chart_role: Browser-rendered OLS states I and IV visually inspected: scatter, fitted line and residual squares; IV table n=11, slope=.50, intercept=3.00. Initial empty axes require reader selection.
prose_structure: Instructional definitions, controls, parameter explanations; no news claim.
learning_objective_interaction: Select I/IV verified; visible data and fitted summary changed. Dragging, correlation matrix, ANOVA and touch/keyboard accessibility not exercised.
adaptation_feasibility_effort: Low for an original static quartet guide; medium for an accessible draggable demonstration with resets, instructions and numerical checks. Existing small datasets suffice.
licensing: Repository LICENSE is Apache-2.0; hosted dataset-specific provenance/reuse notice not separately verified. Check data origins and deployed-version correspondence before copying code or data.
unresolved_issues: Chapter explicitly archived. Browser selection verified, not all interactions. No blanket claim that website prose/images/datasets inherit every code licence term.
craft_lesson: Let one controlled change alter both picture and statistic; a guided prediction/check is stronger than an unexplained widget. Provide an informative default state and accessible fallback.

title: For Example
author: Mike Bostock
format_length: Illustrated talk transcript, 2013-06-06 talk adapted for web; not a NYT graphics survey
question: What makes an example communicate why a technical idea matters?
claim: Examples need audience context and concrete utility; the essay dissects an initially under-explained projection demonstration.
comparison_denominator: No statistical population denominator. Relevant comparisons are alternative rendering methods, scales and map rotations; demonstrations are evidence with selected boundary cases.
data_coverage_units: Projection geometry/code examples and later practitioner graphics. Historical bl.ocks embeds identified in HTML; original exact input geometry/code not recovered.
analysis: Problem -> naive alternative -> adaptive resampling -> practical artifacts -> broader objection. This is explanatory reasoning, not a general empirical test of communication outcomes.
argument_sequence_counterevidence: Starts with a flawed example, restores concepts/purpose, tests representative applications, considers alternatives, then discusses tools and practice. Selected demos cannot prove universal superiority.
chart_role: Text and static montage/NYT screenshots load; projection iframe shows failure icon in headless browser. Dynamic map behavior not verified.
prose_structure: Talk-like sections; explanation repeatedly returns to a concrete example.
learning_objective_interaction: Learn to connect mechanism with use. Rotatable-map instruction exists, but historic interactive did not render; code inspection and interaction remain unresolved.
adaptation_feasibility_effort: Low/medium for an original line-chart before/after guide using an existing dataset; high/unresolved to restore historical projection demonstrations and dependencies.
licensing: Essay/static graphics and individual gists have separate rights; no blanket licence established. Public view-source/fork links are not themselves reuse permission.
unresolved_issues: Static illustrations accessible; historical interactive/code/data not recovered. Preserve correction: visual explanation with practitioner examples, not a systematic NYT graphics survey or Tufte book review.
craft_lesson: Explain what the reader is seeing and why it matters before the mechanism. Include a plausible failed alternative; choose examples for relevance, not visual spectacle.
